one_liner: A narrow-moat business worth owning, but it trades at 1.4x fair value. Interesting below about $163.

profile.what: Royal Caribbean Group owns the Royal Caribbean International, Celebrity Cruises and Silversea brands and a share of two European lines, and operates private destinations in the Caribbean.
profile.money: Passengers pay for the cruise and then spend more on board. Newer, larger ships earn higher returns than older ones.
profile.valued: Royal Caribbean is valued on P/E and EV/EBITDA. The multiple moves with bookings, pricing and confidence in consumer travel spending.

summary.sentence: The best-run cruise line, earning record profits on a still-leveraged balance sheet.
strengths: Earnings per share have risen for three years.
Gross margin has widened every year since fiscal 2022.
Operating cash flow has risen every year since fiscal 2022.
risks: Debt is about twice shareholders' equity.
Current liabilities are several times current assets.

meaning.what_it_does: The second-largest cruise company, operating Royal Caribbean, Celebrity and Silversea ships and its own private island destinations.
meaning.how_it_makes_money: Ticket sales, plus on-board spending on drinks, excursions, casinos and internet.
meaning.how_it_keeps_making_money: New, very large ships and private destinations command higher prices than rivals and than comparable holidays on land.
meaning.how_it_could_stop: A recession, health scare or fuel shock empties ships that are financed with heavy debt.

moat.summary: The best-regarded large cruise brand with the newest ships, in an industry with heavy fixed costs and few competitors.

industry.summary: Cruising changes slowly, but demand is sensitive to the economy and to shocks.

management.summary: Rebuilt the balance sheet quickly after the pandemic and resumed dividends and buybacks.

financial_health.ratio_gaps: Not available from the data source, so not shown: a ten-year record, inventory and receivables turnover, the quick ratio, goodwill and tangible book value, and maintenance capex split from growth capex. Owner earnings therefore deduct all capex, which is conservative.

valuation.method: Fair value is the average of two methods: (1) Owner cash flow, capex held at depreciation: $4.0B a year: operating cash flow less depreciation and stock-based pay (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM). Capex is running at 3.0x depreciation, so most of it is expansion, not upkeep. (2) Damodaran: cash flow to the firm: Sales grow 6–12% for five years, fading to 3%; operating margin held at 28%; cost of capital 8.6%. Cash added, debt subtracted. The owner cash flow method grows the cash for five years, then at half that rate, 3% after year ten, discounted at 10%. Stock-based pay is deducted because it is a real cost to owners.
